reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 1 introduces a novel formulation of the good arm identification problem within a stochastic multi-armed bandit framework, extending classical single-objective settings to multi-objective scenarios. Each arm yields an M-dimensional reward vector rather than a scalar, necessitating a vectorial comparison against a predefined threshold vector ξ. An arm is deemed ε-good if its expected reward vector exceeds ξ minus ε in every component. The paper proposes the MultiTUCB algorithm, which extends Upper Confidence Bound principles to this multi-threshold context. It leverages concentration inequalities to bound the probability of selecting suboptimal arms, ensuring that the final output satisfies the ε-goodness criterion with high probability. The theoretical analysis includes establishing sample complexity bounds and demonstrating near-optimality through lower bounds when ε=0. Empirical validation shows superiority over baseline methods on synthetic and real-world datasets. This work bridges the gap between traditional bandit theory and practical multi-criteria decision-making problems such as IoT deployment or industrial process optimization, where multiple conflicting objectives must be simultaneously satisfied.
